summary: This unit teaches you to receive deliveries and store stock at a villa or hotel: check each delivery against the purchase order and delivery note, test the quantity, quality, condition and temperature of the goods, deal with shortages and damage, put each kind of stock in the right place, rotate stock, keep records and stock cards, keep the store secure and pest-free, and work safely.

blocks.p: Every villa and hotel runs on stock: food and drink, cleaning chemicals, linen, towels and guest amenities such as soap and shampoo. Stock costs money, and some of it (like fresh food) is dangerous if it is handled badly. The person who **receives** stock decides whether the property accepts goods it has paid for, and the person who **stores** it decides whether they stay safe, fresh and available when they are needed.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees who work in stores, kitchens, housekeeping or general administration. You will work with paperwork, simple numbers and food safety, and you will lift and carry goods.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Prepare for deliveries
Know what is expected and when
Have space, staff and paperwork ready
Check a delivery
Compare goods with the purchase order and the delivery note
Check quantity, quality, condition, dates and temperature
Deal with problems
Short, wrong, damaged or out-of-date goods
Reject, record, report and get a credit note
Store each kind of stock correctly
Dry, chilled, frozen, chemicals, linen, amenities and liquor
Rotate stock: first in, first out
Keep records
Stock cards, delivery notes, requisitions
Stocktakes and reorder levels
Keep the store secure, clean and pest-free
Locked stores, key log, signed requisitions
Cleaning, pest checks
Work safely
Lift and carry safely, use trolleys and ladders correctly
Handle chemicals and sharp tools safely

flow: Prepare for the delivery
Check against the paperwork
Check quantity, quality, condition and temperature
Accept or reject, and sign
Put away at once, perishables first
Record the stock
Rotate, check, and keep the store clean and secure

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks: you receive a mixed delivery with hidden problems, check it against the paperwork, then organise a store room and carry out a stocktake. The assessor watches your checking, your decisions on faulty goods, your storage, your hygiene and safety, and your records.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practice use the Centre's mock deliveries and store. Never take real stock home or eat practice food that has been left out.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The person who receives stock should know **when deliveries are expected**, so that space, staff and paperwork are ready in time. Without this, chilled goods wait in the sun while the receiver looks for the paperwork.

head: Get ready
Why
rows: The **purchase order (PO)**: the property's own list of what it ordered, with quantities and prices
It is what you check the delivery against.
A clean, clear **receiving area**, with a table or scales and light
So goods can be checked properly, off the floor and away from the weather.
Cold space in the fridge and freezer for chilled and frozen goods
Cold goods must be put away straight after checking.
Trolley, sack truck, probe thermometer, pen and a calculator
To move and check the goods.
Someone trained and allowed to receive stock
Only they should sign for deliveries.
Your own hygiene: clean hands, apron, hair tied back, no jewellery that falls off
You will handle food.

head: Document
Who makes it
What it shows
Use
rows: **Purchase order**
The property
What was ordered: items, quantity, price.
Check the delivery against it.
**Delivery note** (delivery docket)
The supplier
What the supplier says it has sent.
Count the goods against it; sign it only when you have checked.
**Invoice**
The supplier
What the property owes: items, prices, total and GCT.
Check it against the PO and the delivery note, then send it for payment.
**Credit note**
The supplier
An amount taken off what the property owes, for goods returned, short or damaged.
Make sure the property is not charged for rejected goods.
**Requisition**
A department
A signed request for stock from the store.
Issue stock only against a signed one.
**Stock card (bin card)**
The store
A record of stock received, issued and left for one item.
Keep it up to date.

blocks.p: **GCT** on an invoice is the General Consumption Tax, charged at the current rate set by law. Check that the invoice shows it correctly.

blocks.note: Your signature on a delivery note says the goods arrived as listed. **Check before you sign.** Once you have signed, it is hard to claim for a shortage or damage.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Every delivery is checked for three things: **quantity** (the right number), **quality** (the right standard and freshness) and **condition** (undamaged and safe).

flow: Wash your hands, put on your apron, and meet the driver
Check chilled and frozen goods **first**, so they do not warm up
Compare the goods with the delivery note and the purchase order
Count the items and check the sizes and brands
Look at the quality, the condition and the packaging
Check the dates on food labels
Record any problem on the delivery note, and have the driver sign it
Sign for the goods you accept
Put the goods away at once

head: Check
What to look for
rows: Quantity
Count cases and items. Open a few boxes to check the contents match the label. Check weights on scales.
Quality
Fresh smell and colour; right grade and size; correct brand and specification.
Condition
Boxes dry and undamaged; cans not dented, swollen or leaking; bottles sealed; no signs of pests; towels and linen clean and dry.
Dates

**Use-by date**: the last day the food is safe to eat. **Best-before date**: the food is best before then but is not dangerous just after. Reject anything past its use-by date, and anything with an unreadable or torn label.
Temperature
Use a clean, checked **probe thermometer** (see below).
Cleanliness of the vehicle and driver
A clean van, with chilled and frozen goods kept cold.

head: Food
Safe temperature on delivery (or as the Centre's food safety plan says)
rows: Chilled food (fresh meat, fish, chicken, milk, cooked meats)
**5 °C or below.** Above 5 °C, bacteria can grow fast.
Frozen food
Hard frozen, at about **−18 °C**; a reading warmer than about −15 °C is usually rejected. Signs of thawing: soft food, ice crystals, water or blood in the box, boxes stuck together.
Dry goods (rice, flour, tins)
No temperature check; look for damage and dates.

flow: Clean and sanitise the probe with an alcohol wipe
Check that the thermometer is accurate, as your plan says (for example in iced water, about 0 °C)
Push the tip into the middle of the product, or between two packs of wrapped food
Wait until the reading is steady
Write down the temperature, the item and the time
Clean the probe again before the next item

ul: If chilled goods are above 5 °C, **reject them**, or follow the property's plan, which may allow a short time to check with a supervisor.
A delivery van that has stood in the sun with warm boxes: check the temperature of the food. If it is too warm, reject it.
Frozen shrimp that is soft, with ice crystals and water in the box, has probably thawed and been refrozen. Reject it: it may be unsafe.

blocks.note: Never accept chilled or frozen food that is outside its safe temperature just to avoid a quarrel or to save the villa money. Food poisoning harms guests and can close a business.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Item
Reject if
rows: Canned food
Dented badly (especially on the seam), **swollen or blown** (the ends bulge out), leaking, rusty or with no label.
Fresh meat and fish
Smells bad, feels slimy or sticky, has a grey or green colour, or is warm.
Fruit and vegetables
Mouldy, crushed, wet, wilted or covered with insects.
Eggs
Cracked, dirty or damp.
Dry goods
Torn bags, signs of insects or mice, damp, past the date.
Bottles and cartons
Broken seals, leaks, damage, or past the date.
Chemicals
Leaking containers, no label, or a wrong product.
Linen and towels
Wet, dirty, torn, wrong size or colour, or smelling of mould.

sections.title: When something is wrong with the delivery

head: Problem
What you do
rows: Short (fewer than on the delivery note)
Write the number **actually received** on the delivery note
Have the driver sign next to it
Report it, so that the supplier sends the rest or issues a credit note
Wrong item
Do not accept it; record it on the delivery note
Tell the supervisor; the supplier collects it and sends the right item
Damaged goods
Reject them; record the damage on the delivery note
Take photographs if the property's rule allows
Past its date, or too warm
Reject; record the reason on the note
Tell the supervisor
Leaking chemicals
Reject the leaking one; keep it apart; clean up as the SDS says (see Safety)
More than ordered
Do not accept extra without the supervisor's approval; it will be invoiced
Goods that were not ordered at all
Do not accept; tell the supervisor

flow: Stop and do not sign for the faulty goods
Show the driver the problem
Write it on the delivery note (or the supplier's rejection form) and have the driver sign
Separate the faulty goods from the good ones, and label them 'Returned' or 'Rejected'
Tell your supervisor
Make sure the supplier issues a **credit note** so that the property does not pay for them

ul: A **credit note** is a document from the supplier that reduces what the villa owes. If goods are sent back and the villa gets no credit note, it will pay for goods it never kept.
When the invoice comes, check it against the **PO and the delivery note**: item, quantity, price and GCT. If it charges for goods rejected or not received, query it before it is paid.
Rejecting goods politely and firmly is part of the job. You are protecting the guests and the property.

blocks.p: A delivery note says 12 cases of tinned tomatoes. The driver brings 12, but you reject 3 damaged cases. You accept **9** cases. On the delivery note you write '9 received, 3 rejected (dented)' and the driver signs. Later the invoice shows 12 cases at J$4,200 a case. You should ask for a credit note for 3 × J$4,200 = J$12,600.

blocks.note: When you reject goods, write down **what** was wrong, **how many**, and **who** (the driver) saw it. A clear record makes the credit note easy and the supplier fair.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Put away **chilled and frozen foods first**, so that they stay cold. Then fresh produce, then dry goods, then chemicals and other items. Do not leave a delivery standing in the receiving area.

head: Stock
Where and how
rows: Dry food (rice, flour, tins, ackee, sugar)
**Dry store**: clean, dry, cool, well aired and away from sunlight
On shelves or pallets, off the floor (a common guide is at least 15 cm)
Opened packs go into labelled, covered containers
Chilled food
Fridge or cool room at **5 °C or below**
Covered and labelled; **raw meat and fish on the bottom shelf**, below cooked and ready-to-eat food
Do not overfill, so cold air can move
Frozen food
Freezer at about **−18 °C or colder**
Wrapped and labelled with the date; do not refreeze food that has thawed
Fresh fruit and vegetables
Cool, dry and airy; some in the fridge
Keep onions away from other foods that can take in the smell
Cleaning chemicals
**Separate, locked store**, away from food
Low shelves, in their original containers, with labels and the safety data sheet (SDS) nearby
Linen and towels
Clean, dry, aired store, on shelves, off the floor
Guest amenities (soap, shampoo, slippers)
Dry store or cupboard, on shelves; locked if valuable
Liquor and valuable stock
**Locked** liquor store; keys controlled and signed out

ul: **Heavy items** (cases of drinks, sacks) go on **low shelves**, so they are safe to lift. Light items go higher.
Keep **strong-smelling items** such as onions, fish and cleaning products away from flour, rice and linen, which take in smells.
Keep food, chemicals and linen **apart** from each other.
Keep walkways and fire exits clear. Do not stack boxes against the wall so that air cannot circulate or against sprinklers or lights.

head: Method
What it means
How to do it
rows: **FIFO** (first in, first out)
The oldest stock is used first.
Put new stock **behind or below** the old, so that the old is used first.
**FEFO** (first expired, first out)
The stock that expires first is used first, even if it arrived later.
Check the dates when putting away; place the earliest date at the front.

ul: Write the **date received** on boxes and containers. When you move food into store containers, label it with the **name and the date** so that staff know what it is and use it in date order.
Check dates regularly. Take out anything past its date, and record it as waste.
Never mix a new delivery with an old batch in the same container.
Old stock left at the back goes out of date and is wasted, which is wasted money.
Unlabelled food cannot be identified, so it may be used wrongly or thrown away.
Dates protect guests: food used after its use-by date can make people ill.

blocks.note: Jamaica's heat and humidity are hard on stock. Keep dry stores aired and dry; damp makes flour and rice go mouldy and attracts insects. Do not stack stock where the afternoon sun or a hot water heater warms the wall. After a power cut, check the temperature of fridges and freezers before you decide what is safe to keep.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **stock card** is a record of the stock **received, issued and left** for one item. It is kept with the stock or in the store office.

head: Date
Received
Issued
Balance
rows: 1 Nov (opening)
3 Nov
5 Nov

blocks.p: Balance = old balance + received − issued. In the example, 30 + 50 = 80, then 80 − 20 = **60**.

ul: Update the card **every time** stock goes in or out, and write who and which document.
The balance on the card should equal the stock on the shelf.

blocks.h: Requisitions: how stock leaves the store

ul: A **requisition** is a signed request for stock from the store. Issue stock **only** against a signed requisition.
If a co-worker asks for a case of rum or a pack of towels without a signed requisition, **politely refuse** until you have one. It protects you and the property.
Record what you issue, to whom and when. Check the quantity with the person collecting it and have them sign.

blocks.p: A **stocktake** is counting **all stock** and comparing the count with the records.

flow: Choose a time with few movements (stop issues while you count)
Print or prepare the stock card list
Count each item on the shelf, in pairs if possible (one counts, one records)
Write the count on the stocktake sheet
Compare it with the stock card balance
Recount any difference
Report differences to the supervisor with the reason if known
Correct the records only as the supervisor approves

ul: A stocktake finds **shortages** (theft, waste, errors), **excess** and **out-of-date or slow-moving** items.
If you find fewer bottles than the card shows, **recount, then report the difference** to the supervisor. Do not change the card to match, and do not make up the difference from your own pocket.
Stocktakes are done regularly: weekly or monthly for most items, and daily for high-value items such as liquor.

blocks.p: Order before stock runs out, so the villa never has to refuse a guest something it should have. Most stores use two figures.

head: Term
What it means
Example
rows: **Reorder level**
The stock level at which you must order more.
Weekly use 30 bottles; supplier takes 1 week; keep 20 as a safety margin. Reorder level = (30 × 1) + 20 = **50**.
**Par stock**
The amount you want to have on hand after a delivery.
Par 120; you have 45; order 120 − 45 = **75**.
**Lead time**
How long the supplier takes to deliver.
One week.

ul: Use your sales or use records, the **bookings** for the next weeks, and the time the supplier needs to deliver.
In the busy **tourist season** (roughly mid-December to April), order earlier and more, check you have the space, and talk to suppliers about their own stock before the rush.
In the slow season, order less so that stock does not go out of date.
Do not buy more than you can store safely or use before it expires.
**Lock** the store, especially the liquor store and the guest amenities store. They are locked because valuable stock can be stolen.
Keep a **key log**: a book or sheet showing who has signed out each store key, and when it was returned.
Allow only authorised people in. Do not leave the store open when you are away.
Issue stock only against signed requisitions.
Keep delivery doors shut when not in use; do not let drivers wander into the store.
Report missing stock, broken locks or strangers at once.
Sweep and mop the floor regularly; wipe shelves; clear spills at once.
Take out cardboard and rubbish: cardboard hides insects. Store food off the floor, so the floor can be cleaned.
Keep the store cool, dry and aired. Check for leaks and damp.
Wash and dry shelves before putting new stock on them.

head: Sign of pests
What it means
What to do
rows: Droppings, chewed bags or boxes
Rats or mice
Remove the damaged stock; **report at once**; clean up safely with gloves.
Live or dead insects, webs, a stale smell in dry goods
Cockroaches, ants, weevils
Remove and discard affected stock; report; clean the shelf.
Gnawed wires, nests, dirty marks along the walls
Rats
Report so that the pest control company can come.
Flies near food or bins
Poor waste handling
Cover waste; clean bins; report.

ul: Never use pesticide or poison yourself near food. Pest control is done by trained people.
Keep the doors and windows closed or screened, and block gaps.
Good housekeeping (clean, dry, off the floor, covered food) is the best protection against pests.
**Wash your hands** well and put on a clean apron before handling fresh food.
Tie your hair back; do not handle food when you are sick, or with open cuts that are not covered.
Keep raw and cooked food apart, always.
Use clean, covered containers.
Use a **trolley or sack truck** (a two-wheeled hand truck) for heavy or bulky goods: a delivery of 20 kg bags of rice goes on a trolley, and each bag is lifted with bent knees.
Lift with your **knees bent and back straight**, holding the load close. Do not twist. If it is too heavy, get help.
Stack boxes so that they are steady and cannot fall. Put heavy goods low.
Wear **safety boots** or strong closed shoes, and gloves for rough or wet goods.
Use a **pallet** (a flat wooden or plastic platform) for heavy stacks, and a pallet jack only if you are trained.

flow: Check the weight and the route
Clear the path of obstacles and spills
Stand close, feet apart, knees bent, back straight
Lift with your legs and keep the load close
Move without twisting
Put down the same way

ul: Open cardboard boxes with a box cutter: cut **away from you**, cut only deep enough for the tape, and **close the blade** when you have finished. Never leave it open.
To reach a high shelf, use a **checked step stool or stepladder** on a flat floor. Never climb on boxes, crates or a chair, and never overreach.
Do not store heavy items on high shelves.

blocks.p: Every cleaning chemical has a **safety data sheet (SDS)** that tells you the hazards, the safe handling, first aid and what to do in a spill. Keep the SDS where staff can reach it.

flow: Read the label and the SDS
Put on gloves (and eye protection if the SDS says)
Stop the leak if you can, and keep the container upright
Keep it **apart** from other stock, and from food
Mop up as the SDS says; never mix chemicals
Report it, and record the spill

blocks.note: Never mix bleach with other cleaning chemicals. Some mixtures give off poisonous gas. If you smell a strong gas, leave the area and get fresh air, and tell your supervisor.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Keep the doors shut so cold air stays in and food stays safe; check the thermometer daily and record it.
Never get shut inside a cool room: know where the inside release is, and work with a colleague.
Wet floors in the cold room are slippery: wipe them up and wear non-slip shoes.
I can prepare for a delivery: space, staff and paperwork.
I can name the purchase order, delivery note, invoice, credit note, requisition and stock card, and say what each is for.
I can check quantity, quality, condition and dates, and sign only after checking.
I can check the temperature of chilled and frozen food with a clean probe, and reject food that is too warm.
I can spot dented, blown or leaking cans, thawed frozen food and damaged goods.
I can deal with a short, wrong or damaged delivery, and get a credit note.
I can put stock away in the right place: dry, chilled, frozen, chemicals, linen, amenities and liquor.
I can rotate stock with FIFO and FEFO, and label food with name and date.
I can keep and update a stock card, and work out the balance.
I can issue stock only against signed requisitions, and report stocktake differences.
I can work out a reorder level and an order quantity.
I can keep the store secure, clean and pest-free.
I can lift, carry and use box cutters, ladders and chemicals safely.

terms: Purchase order
The property's own list of what it ordered.
Delivery note (docket)
The supplier's list of the goods sent.
Invoice
The supplier's bill for the goods.
Credit note
A document from the supplier reducing what the property owes.
Requisition
A signed request for stock from the store.
Stock card (bin card)
A record of stock received, issued and left for one item.
Stocktake
Counting all stock and comparing it with the records.
Reorder level
The stock level at which more must be ordered.
Par stock
The amount you want on hand after a delivery.
FIFO
First in, first out: older stock is used before newer.
FEFO
First expired, first out: the stock that expires first is used first.
Use-by date
The last day food is safe to eat.
Best-before date
The date until which food is at its best quality.
Perishable
Food, such as milk, meat and fish, that goes bad quickly unless kept cold.
Probe thermometer
A thermometer with a metal tip, used to check food temperature.
Blown can
A can whose ends bulge out; it must be rejected.
Pallet
A flat platform that heavy goods are stacked on.
Sack truck
A two-wheeled hand truck for heavy sacks and boxes.
SDS
Safety data sheet for a chemical.
Key log
A record of who has signed out each store key.
Pests
Animals and insects such as rats, mice and cockroaches.
GCT
General Consumption Tax; shown on invoices at the current rate set by law.

c1.title: A delivery at a Negril villa
c1.text: At 8:30 a.m. a supplier's van arrives at a villa in Negril. The delivery note lists 12 cases of ginger beer, 6 trays of chicken and a box of dish soap. Storekeeper Camille counts 10 cases of ginger beer. A probe thermometer put into the middle of a pack of chicken reads 9 °C. The driver is in a hurry and offers to bring the missing cases tomorrow.

c2.title: The dry store at a guest house
c2.text: While putting away a delivery in the dry store of a guest house in Mandeville, trainee Rohan finds a tin of ackee with swollen ends, a bag of flour with a small chewed hole and mouse droppings on the shelf below it, and two batches of tinned ackee: the old one with a best-before date of June and the new one with a date of December.

c3.title: Cards and a requisition in the store
c3.text: The villa's stock card for body lotion shows an opening balance of 40 bottles. A delivery of 60 bottles arrives and housekeeping later collects 25 on a signed requisition. Separately, a stocktake of the liquor store finds 18 bottles of rum, but the stock card says 20. A bartender asks the storekeeper for a case of rum with no signed requisition, saying the manager told him verbally.

c4.title: Chemicals and a high shelf
c4.text: A delivery to a hotel in Montego Bay includes a box of floor cleaner, a bottle of drain cleaner that is leaking at the cap, a bottle of bleach standing beside it, and cartons of toilet tissue. The storekeeper must put the stock away. The only free space for the tissue is a shelf above head height. A box cutter lies on the table, with its blade out.

c5.title: Ordering before the busy season
c5.text: A villa in Treasure Beach uses about 30 bottles of shampoo a week. Its supplier needs one week to deliver, and the villa wants to keep a safety margin of 20 bottles. The villa's par stock for shampoo is 120 bottles, and it now has 45 on the shelf. Bookings for December and January are much higher than last year.

c6.title: Towels and onions
c6.text: A supplier delivers 40 bath towels to a hotel in Ocho Rios in two cartons. One carton feels damp and smells of mould. At the same time, the cook sends a sack of onions to the store, and the only free shelf is next to the flour and rice.

questions.q: Camille counts 10 cases of ginger beer, but the note says 12. The driver says he will bring the rest tomorrow. What should she do?
o: Sign for 12 now, then check the missing cases when they come tomorrow
Write 10 on the note, have the driver sign, and report it
Take the ginger beer, and correct the note herself later in the day
Refuse the whole delivery, including the chicken and the dish soap
questions.why: A delivery note should show what really arrived. Write the number received, have the driver sign it and report the shortage so that the rest is delivered or a credit note is issued. Signing for 12 would mean the villa accepts goods it did not get.

questions.q: The chicken reads 9 °C in the middle of the pack. What is the correct decision?
o: Accept it, but cook the chicken first thing tomorrow morning
Accept it, since 9 °C is cool enough to keep chicken for a day
Reject it and record the temperature on the note
Accept it, and put it at the back of the fridge to keep it cold
questions.why: Chilled food must be 5 °C or below. At 9 °C bacteria can grow quickly, so the chicken is rejected and the reason is recorded. Cooking it later does not make it safe to have been kept warm.

questions.q: What is the correct way for Camille to take the chicken's temperature?
o: Clean the probe, push it into the middle, wait for a steady reading
Hold the thermometer against the outside of the box for a full minute
Put the probe into the packing liquid at the bottom of the delivery box
Touch the pack with the back of her hand to judge how cold it is
questions.why: Use a clean, checked probe pushed into the centre of the product or between packs, and wait until the reading is steady. Surface or guess checks do not show the real temperature, and the probe must be cleaned again afterwards.

questions.q: Which goods should Camille check first when the van arrives?
o: The dish soap, because it is the lightest item to carry in
The ginger beer, because it is the biggest quantity on the van
The paperwork only, before any of the goods come off the van
The chilled chicken, so it does not warm up
questions.why: Chilled and frozen goods are checked first and put away at once, as they spoil if they stay warm. Dry goods and chemicals can wait a few minutes longer.

questions.q: What should Rohan do with the tin of ackee with swollen ends?
o: Use it first in the next day's breakfast, so that it is not wasted
Set it aside, record it and report it
Open it outside, and use the ackee if it smells all right to her
Put it at the back of the shelf, where it is cooler and out of sight
questions.why: A swollen (blown) tin may contain gas from bacteria and must never be eaten. Remove it from stock, record it and report it, so that the supplier can be asked for a credit.

questions.q: Where should the December ackee go, in relation to the June ackee?
o: Mixed with the June tins on the same shelf, to save on space
On the floor beside the shelf, so that it is out of the way
Behind the June tins, so the June ones go first
In front of the June tins, because the December tins are newer stock
questions.why: Stock with the earlier date is used first (FEFO, a form of first in, first out). New stock goes behind, so that the older tins are taken from the front. Stock on the floor is hard to clean and open to pests.

questions.q: What is the right response to the chewed flour bag and the droppings?
o: Sweep the droppings away, and say nothing to avoid causing worry
Put a box over the hole in the shelf, to stop more mice getting in
Remove the damaged stock, clean up with gloves, report the pests
Put the flour in a new bag, and use it up quickly in the kitchen
questions.why: Droppings and chewed bags mean rodents. Damaged and possibly contaminated stock is removed, the area cleaned safely and pests reported at once, so that trained people can deal with them. Hiding the problem lets it grow.

questions.q: Rohan has a half-used bag of rice. What is the best way to store it?
o: In an open basin on the shelf, so that the rice can breathe
In the fridge, so that insects cannot reach it before it is used
In its torn bag, folded over and tucked in at the back of the shelf
In a clean, covered container with a name and date
questions.why: Opened dry food goes into a clean, covered container with a label and date, so that it stays free from pests and damp and is used in date order. A torn bag or open bowl lets in insects.

questions.q: How many bottles of body lotion should the stock card show now?
questions.why: Balance = opening + received − issued = 40 + 60 − 25 = 75 bottles. The card should match what is on the shelf.

questions.q: What should the storekeeper do about the bartender's request for rum?
o: Ask a colleague to hand over the case instead, so he is not involved
Politely refuse until a signed requisition is brought
Give him half a case now, and ask for the form to be signed later
Give him the case, because the manager has already said it was fine
questions.why: Stock is issued only against a signed requisition, even when someone says it is approved. Refuse politely and explain the rule, and the bartender can get the form signed. This protects the storekeeper and the property.

questions.q: Two careful recounts of the liquor store still give 18 bottles of rum, while the card says 20. What happens to the card?
o: It is changed to 18 at once, so that it matches the shelf
It is changed to 18, and the storekeeper pays for two bottles
It stays as it is until the supervisor approves a correction
It is left alone, and nobody is told until the next stocktake
questions.why: A shortage is reported to the supervisor with the counts, and the records are corrected only on the supervisor's approval. Changing the card quietly hides a possible loss, and paying from your pocket does not explain it.

questions.q: The storekeeper must leave the liquor store for ten minutes. What should he do?
o: Leave the door closed but unlocked, as he will be back very soon
Leave the key in the lock, so that it is easy to find on return
Lock it and keep the key, or sign it back on the log
Ask the bartender to keep an eye on the store while he is out
questions.why: Valuable stock must be locked whenever the storekeeper is away, and the key kept under control, with the key log signed. A store that is left open invites theft.

questions.q: What is the safest first step with the leaking drain cleaner?
o: Mop it up with the same cloth that was used for the floor cleaner
Put on gloves, keep it upright and apart, and follow the SDS
Pour it down the sink, to get rid of the leaking liquid quickly
Put it on the shelf with the other cleaners, where it will be safe
questions.why: A leaking chemical is handled with gloves, kept upright and separate, and cleaned up as its safety data sheet says. Never mix chemicals or use the same cloth, as some mixtures give off poisonous gas.

questions.q: Where should the bleach and the drain cleaner be stored?
o: In the housekeeping cupboard, on the shelf next to the clean towels
Together on one shelf, so that all the cleaners are in one place
In the locked chemical store, apart from each other and food
On the lowest shelf of the food store, tucked in behind the rice
questions.why: Chemicals go in their own locked store, away from food, linen and each other, in their original containers with labels. Bleach and other chemicals can react dangerously if they leak together.

questions.q: How should the storekeeper reach the shelf above head height?
o: Throw the packs up from the floor, one pack at a time, onto the shelf
Climb on a carton of tissue standing near the shelf, to save time
Use a checked step stool or stepladder on a flat floor
Stand on a chair, and hold the edge of the shelf for balance
questions.why: Use a checked stepladder or step stool on a flat floor. Never climb on boxes or chairs. Better still, keep light items such as tissue on high shelves and heavy items low.

questions.q: What is the villa's reorder level for shampoo?
o: 50 bottles
20 bottles
30 bottles
70 bottles
questions.why: Reorder level = use during the supplier's lead time + safety margin = (30 × 1) + 20 = 50 bottles. When stock falls to 50, order more.

questions.q: The villa has 45 bottles and its par stock is 120. How many bottles should it order?
questions.why: Order quantity = par stock − stock on hand = 120 − 45 = 75 bottles.

questions.q: Bookings for December and January are much higher. What is the sensible plan?
o: Wait until the shelves are nearly empty, then order as usual
Order the same amounts as last year to be on the safe side
Cut the safety margin, so that less stock is held on the shelf
Order earlier and more, if there is room to store it
questions.why: A busy season needs more stock and earlier orders, because suppliers may run short. Check the storage space and expiry dates, so you do not over-order.

questions.q: What should the storekeeper do about the damp, musty carton of towels?
o: Store the carton on the top shelf of the linen store to dry out
Reject it, record the reason and have the driver sign
Accept the carton, and hang the towels out in the sun to dry
Accept the carton, and wash the towels before they are used
questions.why: Damp, mouldy linen is a faulty delivery. Reject it and record the reason, so that the supplier replaces it. Storing damp towels spreads mould to the rest of the linen.

questions.q: Where should the sack of onions be stored?
o: In the linen store, where it is dry and the shelves are clean
Next to the flour and rice, on the one shelf that is free
Away from the flour and rice, in a cool, airy place
In the freezer, where the onions will keep fresh for longer
questions.why: Flour, rice and linen take in smells, so strong-smelling items such as onions are kept away from them. Onions need a cool, airy place.
